Closing the Curvature Gap: Full Transformer Hessians and Their Implications for Scaling Laws

Egor Petrov Affiliation: Yandex, BRAIn Lab Email: moderntalker@yandex-team.ru    Nikita Kiselev Affiliation: Independent Email: bashmak22@gmail.com    Vladislav Meshkov Affiliation: Independent Email: vladmeshkov160@gmail.com    Andrey Grabovoy Affiliation: Moscow State University Email: andriy.graboviy@gmail.com
Abstract

The lack of theoretical results for Layer Normalization and feedforward Hessians has left a gap in the study of Transformer optimization landscapes. We address this by deriving explicit second-order expressions for these components, thereby completing the Hessian characterization of full Transformer blocks. Our results generalize prior self-attention analyses and yield estimations for the role of each sublayer in curvature propagation. We demonstrate how these Hessian structures inform both convergence dynamics and the empirical scaling laws governing large-model performance. Further, we propose a Taylor-expansion–based framework for analyzing loss differences to quantify convergence trajectories. By extending Hessian theory to the full Transformer architecture, this work establishes a new foundation for theoretical and empirical investigations of optimization in large-scale deep learning.

Keywords: Transformer Hessians, Layer Normalization, Scaling laws, Convergence dynamics, Loss landscape, Optimization geometry.

1 Introduction

Transformers [1] have revolutionized deep learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance across natural language processing [2, 3], computer vision [4, 5], Their empirical success is underpinned by predictable improvements in model quality with increased dataset size, as described by neural scaling laws [6]; [7, 8]. However, many domains, such as medical imaging [9] and scientific discovery [10], face severe data constraints where acquiring additional samples is costly or infeasible [11]. This tension necessitates a rigorous theoretical understanding of how dataset size shapes the optimization landscape and influences training dynamics.

Existing theoretical analyses of Transformer optimization landscapes are incomplete. While recent studies have derived Hessian expressions for self-attention mechanisms [12, 13], the full Transformer block—including LayerNorm and feed-forward networks (FFNs)—lacks a comprehensive theoretical characterization [14, 15]. These components critically influence optimization dynamics, such as gradient flow and convergence rates [14, 16], and generalization behavior [17, 18]. Without a complete curvature analysis, our understanding of Transformer training dynamics, convergence properties, and scaling behavior remains limited [19].

In this work, we provide the first complete theoretical analysis of the Hessian for full Transformer blocks, extending beyond prior self-attention analyses [12, 13] to include explicit second-order expressions for LayerNorm and FFNs. Our analysis derives rigorous bounds on how the loss landscape evolves with dataset size, offering a novel framework for understanding landscape stabilization in Transformers. These results have implications for optimization challenges (e.g., vanishing gradients [20]), scaling laws (e.g., compute-optimal training [7, 6]), and critical batch size estimation [21, 22].

Contributions. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We derive the first full Hessian expressions for Transformer blocks, including explicit treatment of LayerNorm and FFNs, filling a critical gap in prior analyses.

  • •

    We establish theoretical bounds on the loss landscape’s evolution with dataset size, providing a rigorous framework for understanding landscape stabilization.

  • •

    We validate our theoretical predictions through experiments on Vision Transformers, demonstrating practical relevance across data regimes.

Our work bridges theoretical deep learning and practical Transformer deployment, enabling new insights into optimization difficulties, efficient scaling strategies, and future theoretical investigations of large-scale deep learning.

Outline. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review related work, categorizing existing research into key topics and highlighting their main contributions. Section 3 introduces the notation and presents preliminary calculations essential for our analysis. In Section 4, we derive theoretical bounds for the norm of the Hessian matrix and the norm of the difference between loss functions. Section 5 provides an empirical study validating these theoretical results. Section 6 discuss and summarize our findings, offering insights and conclusions. Additional experiments are in Appendix A and proofs of theorems are included in Appendices B-D.

2 Related Work

Geometry of Neural Network Loss Landscapes Foundational studies characterize neural loss geometry via Hessians, including class-aligned high-curvature directions [19], random-matrix perspectives on spectra and optimization [23], and connectivity and double-descent phenomena [24, 25, 26, 27], with flattening observed at large learning rates [28]. Our work complements this line by showing how curvature of Transformer blocks changes with dataset size, providing explicit second-order bounds that formalize landscape stabilization under data growth. This links classical geometric insights to a data-scaling axis that was previously qualitative.

Hessian-Based Analysis and Generalization Prior Hessian analyses for fully connected and convolutional networks reveal spectral structure and low effective rank with implications for convergence and smoothness [29, 30]. We extend these ideas to Transformers by deriving explicit LayerNorm/FFN second derivatives and blockwise spectral-norm bounds, thereby closing a missing piece in second-order geometry for this architecture.

Loss Landscapes in Transformers While Transformers [1] have inspired curvature analyses focused on attention [12] and studies of sample complexity, generalization, and stagewise dynamics [31, 17, 32], a full-block second-order treatment has remained incomplete. We provide the missing LayerNorm/FFN Hessians and assemble a complete blockwise Hessian for a Transformer layer, aligning theory with empirical curvature structure. This enables a principled account of how Transformer curvature evolves with data and training.

Dataset Size and Loss Landscape Convergence Work on compute-optimal scaling and sample-related flatness highlights the importance of balancing data and model size [7, 33], and visualization tools hint at stabilization thresholds without theory [34]. Building on Hessian frameworks from other architectures [29, 30] and attention derivatives [12], we derive a second-order bound that decays as 1/k1/k. This yields actionable diagnostics for curvature-aware training and data budgeting in Transformers.

4 Method

In this section, we derive generalized Hessian expressions for the self-attention layer and extend them to a full transformer block, leveraging these to analyze the convergence of the loss function surface as the dataset size increases. Our approach builds on the theoretical framework of [12], adapting and generalizing their results.

4.1 Hessian of the Self-Attention Layer

We begin by analyzing the Hessian of a single self-attention layer with parameters 𝐰={𝐖Q,𝐖K,𝐖V}\mathbf{w}=\{\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V}\} as defined in Equation 1. The empirical loss is defined as:ℒk​(𝐰)=1k​∑i=1kl⁡(𝐅⁡(𝐗i),Targeti)\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}l(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}_{i}),\textbf{Target}_{i}), where l⁡(𝐅⁡(𝐗i),Targeti)l(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}_{i}),\textbf{Target}_{i}) is a Loss function defined above.

The Hessian of ℒk\mathcal{L}_{k} with respect to the parameters 𝐰\mathbf{w} is:

𝐇(k)​(𝐰)=∇𝐰2ℒk​(𝐰)=1k​∑i=1k∇𝐰2li​(𝐰)=1k​∑i=1k𝐇i​(𝐰)\mathbf{H}^{(k)}(\mathbf{w})=\nabla^{2}_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\nabla^{2}_{\mathbf{w}}l_{i}(\mathbf{w})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbf{H}_{i}(\mathbf{w})

where 𝐇k​(𝐰)\mathbf{H}_{k}(\mathbf{w}) is a hessian of the Self-Attention block for 𝐰\mathbf{w} being a pair of matrices from {𝐖Q,𝐖K,𝐖V}\{\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V}\}. It can decomposed using the Gauss-Newton approximation 3:

4.2 Hessian of the Transformer Block

A transformer block extends the self-attention layer with a feed-forward network (FFN), residual connections, and layer normalization. The output is:

𝐘\displaystyle\mathbf{Y} =LayerNorm​(𝐗+𝐅​(𝐗))\displaystyle=\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X})) (4)
𝐙\displaystyle\mathbf{Z} =LayerNorm​(𝐘+FFN​(𝐘)),\displaystyle=\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{Y}+\text{FFN}(\mathbf{Y})), (5)

where FFN​(𝐘)=σ⁡(𝐘𝐖1+𝐛1)​𝐖2+𝐛2\text{FFN}(\mathbf{Y})=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{b}_{2}, with 𝐖1∈ℝdV×dff\mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{V}\times d_{\text{ff}}}, 𝐖2∈ℝdff×dV\mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}\times d_{V}}, b1∈ℝdffb_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}}, b2∈ℝdVb_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{V}}, and σ\sigma as the activation (e.g., ReLU). The LayerNorm​(𝐗)\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{X}) operation is defined as follows. For an input matrix 𝐗∈ℝL×dV\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{V}}, we compute:

  1. 1.

    Feature-wise mean and variance:

    μi=1dV​∑j=1dV𝐗i,j,σi2=1dV​∑j=1dV(𝐗i,j−μi)2,\mu_{i}=\frac{1}{d_{V}}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{V}}\mathbf{X}_{i,j},\quad\sigma_{i}^{2}=\frac{1}{d_{V}}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{V}}(\mathbf{X}_{i,j}-\mu_{i})^{2},

    Normalized output with learnable parameters γ,β∈ℝm\mathbf{\gamma},\mathbf{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}:

    LayerNorm​(𝐗)i,j=γj⋅𝐗i,j−μiσi2+βj.\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{X})_{i,j}=\mathbf{\gamma}_{j}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{X}_{i,j}-\mu_{i}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{i}^{2}}}+\mathbf{\beta}_{j}.

The parameters are 𝐰={𝐖Q,𝐖K,𝐖V,𝐖1,𝐖2,𝐛1,𝐛2,γ,β}\mathbf{w}=\{\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V},\mathbf{W}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{2},\mathbf{b}_{1},\mathbf{b}_{2},\mathbf{\gamma},\mathbf{\beta}\}, where γ\mathbf{\gamma} and β\mathbf{\beta} are the scale and shift parameters of LayerNorm. where where ∂2𝐌∂𝐗2=0\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}}=0, and other terms as derived in the proof.

Proofs and detailed versions for Theorems 2-3 are provided in Appendices C.2 - C.3.

Before providing calculations for the whole Transformer Block we need to introduce an activation function matrix derivative.

Lemma 1 (ReLU derivative and Hessian).

Let 𝐗∈ℝm×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, almost everywhere the following holds:

∂ReLU⁡(𝐗)∂𝐗=diag(vecr(𝟏{𝐗>0})),∂2ReLU⁡(𝐗)∂𝐗2=𝟎.\frac{\partial\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\mathrm{diag}\!\big(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{1}_{\{\mathbf{X}>0\}})\big),\quad\frac{\partial^{2}\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}}=\mathbf{0}.

The proof is in the Appendix D.

Thus, we calculate the derivatives and the Hessian of the proposed Transformer block representation 5 with respect to a square norm Loss, where we put 𝐛1,2=0\mathbf{b}_{1,2}=0 in FFN block for simplicity of subsequent calculations and use ReLU as an activation layer.

Theorem 4 (Transformer block derivative).

For Transformer block from 5 with 𝐒=ReLU​(𝐘𝐖1)​𝐖2+𝐘\mathbf{S}=\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{Y} and 𝐙=LayerNorm⁡(𝐒)\mathbf{Z}=\mathrm{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{S}):

∂𝐙∂𝐖i=𝐉Z⋅{𝐁i,i∈{1,2}𝐉S​Y​𝐆i,i∈{K,Q,V}\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}=\mathbf{J}_{Z}\cdot\begin{cases}\mathbf{B}_{i},&i\in\{1,2\}\\ \mathbf{J}_{SY}\mathbf{G}_{i},&i\in\{K,Q,V\}\end{cases}

where 𝐉Z=∂𝐙∂𝐒\mathbf{J}_{Z}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{S}}, 𝐁i=∂𝐒∂𝐖i\mathbf{B}_{i}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}, 𝐉S​Y=∂𝐒∂𝐘\mathbf{J}_{SY}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}, 𝐆i=∂𝐘∂𝐖i\mathbf{G}_{i}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{Y}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}.

More detailed of the theorem and it’s proof can be found in Appendix C.4.

Theorem 5 (Hessian of the Transformer block 5).

The Hessian blocks of the Transformer output 𝐙\mathbf{Z} w.r.t. parameters (𝐖i,𝐖j)(\mathbf{W}_{i},\mathbf{W}_{j}) are

𝐇tr(i,j):=∂2𝐙∂𝐖i​∂𝐖j=(𝐉Z⊗𝐈ni)​𝝃i​j+(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐁i⊤)​𝐇Z​𝐁j\boxed{\;\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}:=\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}=\left(\mathbf{J}_{Z}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{i}}\right)\bm{\xi}_{ij}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{i}^{\top}\right)\mathbf{H}_{Z}\mathbf{B}_{j}\;} (6)

with 𝛏i​j:=∂∂𝐖j​(∂𝐒∂𝐖i)\bm{\xi}_{ij}:=\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}\right), 𝐉Z:=∂LayerNorm⁡(𝐒)∂𝐒,𝐇Z:=∂2LayerNorm⁡(𝐒)∂𝐒2\mathbf{J}_{Z}:=\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{S})}{\partial\mathbf{S}},\mathbf{H}_{Z}:=\frac{\partial^{2}\,\mathrm{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{S})}{\partial\mathbf{S}^{2}} and 𝐁i:=∂𝐒∂𝐖i\mathbf{B}_{i}:=\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}, where 𝐒:=ReLU​(𝐘𝐖1)​𝐖2+𝐘\mathbf{S}:=\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{Y}

More detailed version of the theorem and the proof can be found in Appendix C.5.

We note that the theorem above is responsible for the ∂2f𝐰∂𝐖i​∂𝐖j\frac{\partial^{2}f_{\mathbf{w}}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}} part from the Hessian of the Loss function decomposition 3. Therefore, the whole Transformer Hessian can be represented as:

∂2(ℒ∘𝐙)∂𝐖i​∂𝐖j=∂𝐙∂𝐖i⊤​∂2ℒ∂𝐙2​∂𝐙∂𝐖j+(∂ℒ∂𝐙​(𝐙⁡(⋅))⊗𝐈pi​qi)​𝐇tr(i,j),\frac{\partial^{2}(\mathcal{L}\circ\mathbf{Z})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}^{\top}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{Z}^{2}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}+\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{Z}(\cdot))\otimes\mathbf{I}_{p_{i}q_{i}}\right)\mathbf{H}_{\text{tr}}^{(i,j)}, (7)

where ℒ(⋅)=∥⋅−Target∥22\mathcal{L}(\cdot)=\|\cdot-\textbf{Target}\|^{2}_{2}, it’s second derivative is 2L​dV\frac{2}{Ld_{V}}, and ∂ℒ∂𝐙​(𝐙​(⋅))\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{Z}(\cdot)) can be calculated similarly to 𝐑m\mathbf{R}_{m} from Theorem 3.2 [12], thus, 𝐑mtr=vecr​(𝐙−Target)⊤⊗𝐈m\mathbf{R}^{\text{tr}}_{m}=\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{Z}-\textbf{Target})^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{m}, while ∂𝐙∂𝐖i,∂𝐙∂𝐖j\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}},\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}} are from Theorem 4 and 𝐇tr(i,j)\mathbf{H}_{\text{tr}}^{(i,j)} is from Theorem 5.

Therefore the transformer-block square-norm can be estimated according to the theorem

Theorem 6 (Spectral-norm estimate of the Transformer Hessian).

Let 𝐇tr(i,j)\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)} denote the (i,j)(i,j)-th block of the Transformer Hessian from equation 6, where i,j∈{1,2,K,Q,V}i,j\in\{1,2,K,Q,V\} and ni=dim(𝐖i)n_{i}=\dim(\mathbf{W}_{i}). Then, for each pair (i,j)(i,j),

‖𝐇tr(i,j)‖2≤‖𝐉Z‖2​‖𝝃i​j‖2+‖𝐁i‖2​‖𝐇Z‖2​‖𝐁j‖2,\big\|\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}\big\|_{2}\;\leq\;\|\mathbf{J}_{Z}\|_{2}\,\|\bm{\xi}_{ij}\|_{2}\;+\;\|\mathbf{B}_{i}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{H}_{Z}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{B}_{j}\|_{2}, (8)

where 𝛏i​j=∂∂𝐖j​(∂𝐒∂𝐖i)\bm{\xi}_{ij}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}\!\left(\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}\right) and 𝐁i=∂𝐒∂𝐖i\mathbf{B}_{i}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}.

Explicit expressions for each bound are stated in the proof.

Furthermore, estimation for the whole transformer Hessian can be calculated as:

Let 𝐇tr\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}} be the full Hessian arranged as a mb×nbm_{b}\times n_{b} block-matrix with blocks 𝐇tr(i,j)\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}, where mb=nb=5m_{b}=n_{b}=5 (indexed by {1,2,K,Q,V}\{1,2,K,Q,V\}). Then

‖𝐇tr‖2≤mb​nb​maxi,j⁡(2L​dV​‖∂𝐙∂𝐖i‖2​‖∂𝐙∂𝐖j‖2+‖𝐑mtr‖2​‖𝐇tr(i,j)‖2).\|\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\sqrt{m_{b}n_{b}}\;\max\limits_{i,j}\left(\frac{2}{Ld_{V}}\|\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}\|_{2}\|\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}\|_{2}+\|\mathbf{R}^{\text{tr}}_{m}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{H}_{\text{tr}}^{(i,j)}\|_{2}\right). (9)

Since mb=nb=5m_{b}=n_{b}=5, we get ‖𝐇tr‖2≤5​maxi,j⁡(⋯)\|\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}\|_{2}\leq 5\;\max_{i,j}(\cdots). We denote this estimation as MtrM_{\text{tr}}.

The proof is provided in Appendix C.6.

4.3 Convergence of the Loss Function Surface

Similarly to [29] let us use second-order Taylor approximation for the mentioned above loss functions at 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*}. We suppose that decomposition to the second order will be sufficient to study local behavior. The first-order term vanishes because the gradients ∇ℒk​(𝐰∗)\nabla\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) and ∇ℒk+1​(𝐰∗)\nabla\mathcal{L}_{k+1}(\mathbf{w}^{*}) are zero according to Assumption 1:

ℒk​(𝐰)≈ℒk​(𝐰∗)+12​(𝐰−𝐰∗)⊤​𝐇(k)​(𝐰∗)​(𝐰−𝐰∗),\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w})\approx\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w}^{*})+\dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^{*})^{\top}\mathbf{H}^{(k)}(\mathbf{w}^{*})(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^{*}), (10)

where we denoted the Hessian of ℒk​(𝐰)\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w}) with respect to parameters 𝐰\mathbf{w} at 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} as 𝐇(k)​(𝐰∗)\mathbf{H}^{(k)}(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

Next, we consider difference of losses |ℒk+1​(𝐰)−ℒk​(𝐰)|\left|\mathcal{L}_{k+1}(\mathbf{w})-\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w})\right| while increasing the sequence length.

Theorem 7 (Convergence of Self-Attention and Transformer Blocks).

For a single self-attention block and a single transformer block 5 under the conditions that the loss function is bounded 0⩽l⁡(𝐟𝐰∗​(𝐱i),𝐲i)⩽L0\leqslant l(\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{w}^{*}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}),\mathbf{y}_{i})\leqslant L, and the individual Hessians are bounded, the following holds:

|ℒk+1​(𝐰)−ℒk​(𝐰)|⩽2​Lk+1+M​‖𝐰−𝐰∗‖22(k+1),\left|\mathcal{L}_{k+1}(\mathbf{w})-\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w})\right|\leqslant\dfrac{2L}{k+1}+\dfrac{M\left\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^{*}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{(k+1)},

where for the self-attention block MM can be directly calculated from Theorem 1 and for the transformer block M=MtrM=M_{\text{tr}} is calculated according to Theorem 6.

It’s worth noting that MM in the theorem above is not a constant in terms of increasing the sequence length kk, as soon as MM is a function of ‖𝐗‖2\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2} which changes during described process. For more details see Appendix C.1 and C.6.

The proof is provided in Appendix C.7.

5 Experiments

To verify our theoretical estimates we conduct a comprehensive empirical study. We follow the same Transformer architecture we used in the main part of the paper, which is essentially post-norm (LayerNorm is after Self-Attention/FeedForward).

In particular, we consider an image classification task, implementing the Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture similar to [35], see Figure 2. Input image is patchified with linear projection and then goes to Transformer Encoder, which contains LL Transformer Blocks, while its outputs is averaged to obtain classification logits.

Hessian entries visualization. In this part we use a single Transformer block, which we train on a MNIST [36] dataset (see 1). Firstly, we put just one batch from a train dataloader to the initialized model and calculate the exact Hessian using curvlinops Python package for an efficient Hessian linear operator calculation. Visualizing it in a log-scale, in Figure 3 we emphasize the heterogenity in the magnitues of the entries.

We train the model for a number of epochs, obtaining pretty high accuracy on a validation dataset (>50%), and then visualize the Hessian’s entries again, see Figure 4. One can see that each of the Hessian’s blocks becomes more magnituted, however the Values-Values block exhibits the highest one.

This experiment shows exactly how the entire Transformer’s Hessian is organized, which allows us to investigate each block part of it separately. In Appendix A.1 we continue this experiment by providing Parameters blocks changing over training epochs figures.

Further, we calculate the matrices’ norms and their Hessians’ norms, and show them in Figure 5

Results show that the highest magnitude corresponds to the Keys and Values, while the other blocks exhibit much smaller absolute entries.

Loss landscape convergence. To further deep inside the dependence between loss function and its Hessian, we conduct and experiment corresponding to Theorem 7. Here we employ the other model configuration on a CIFAR-100 [37] dataset. Compared to similar one for a MNIST dataset, this model have 8×8\times more Transformer blocks and also 8×8\times wider hidden layers. During traning, it is also trained for a number of epochs to achieve >50% Accuracy on a validation dataset. The results are in Figure 6. The experiment setup is as follows:

  1. 1.

    Train the model until convergence and save the parameters 𝐰∗\mathbf{w*} (model checkpoint);

  2. 2.

    Start from the empty dataset, add data batch-by-batch and calculate mean loss value over the seen batches;

  3. 3.

    Calculate the absolute difference according to |ℒk+1​(𝐰)−ℒk​(𝐰)|\left|\mathcal{L}_{k+1}(\mathbf{w})-\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w})\right|.

Our code is available at https://github.com/modernTalker/transformer_hessian.git

6 Discussion and Conclusion

This work fills a key gap in the second-order analysis of Transformers by deriving explicit Jacobians and Hessians for LayerNorm and FFN in the vecr\mathrm{vec}_{r} numerator-layout, and integrating them into a full block-level curvature decomposition. Theorems 2-3 and 4-5 yield end-to-end expressions that are compatible with Kronecker structure and commutation identities, while Theorems 1 and 6 provide spectral-norm bounds that connect curvature to input statistics, LayerNorm scales, and architectural hyperparameters. A direct consequence is a block-heterogeneous Hessian: Value- and Key-related terms dominate through softmax derivatives and input-dependent operators, FFN curvature is controlled by the piecewise linearity of ReLU, and LayerNorm contributes via per-row variance. The empirical results (e.g., Figures 3 and 4) match these predictions, with Values - Values blocks exhibiting the largest magnitudes after training.

The second-order Taylor expansion in Theorem 7 gives a compact convergence inequality, |ℒk+1​(𝐰)−ℒk​(𝐰)|≤2​L/(k+1)+M​‖𝐰−𝐰∗‖22/(k+1)|\mathcal{L}_{k+1}(\mathbf{w})-\mathcal{L}_{k}(\mathbf{w})|\leq 2L/(k+1)+M\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}/(k+1), where MM as a function of input data is provided by our Hessian bounds 1, 6. This explains the observed stabilization of the loss landscape with increasing data. The log–log trend in Figure 6 follows this prediction, supporting the claim that increasing data size stabilizes the local geometry of the Transformer objective. Finally, the block-wise structure motivates curvature-aware training through per-block adaptation of learning rates, weight decay, or preconditioning, and provides a mechanistic rationale for switching from data scaling to model scaling near curvature stationarity, consistent with compute-optimal policies [6, 7].

The analysis is local and assumes a shared minimizer for consecutive dataset sizes (Assumption 1). The present theoretical derivation focuses on a single-head, post-normalization transformer block under the mean-squared error loss. While extensions to multi-head attention, masking, and positional encodings are technically feasible within the established calculus, they are omitted for brevity. It should be emphasized that the underlying framework naturally generalizes to the cross-entropy loss, a generalization that has been explicitly validated in our experimental section 5. A primary direction for future work involves extending this analysis to deep, multi-layer transformer architectures.

Appendix B Appendix / Matrix calculus preliminaries

B.1 Basic matrix operations properties

First, we define the notations and rules that we actively use in the text.

Definition 1 (Matrix Norms).

For a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:

‖𝐀‖2\displaystyle\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2} =σ1\displaystyle=\sigma_{1}\quad (Spectral norm, largest singular value)
‖𝐀‖F\displaystyle\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F} =∑i=1m∑j=1n|ai​j|2=∑i=1rσi2\displaystyle=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{ij}|^{2}}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}^{2}}\quad (Frobenius norm)
‖𝐀‖1\displaystyle\|\mathbf{A}\|_{1} =max⁡∑i=1m1≤j≤n⁡|ai​j|\displaystyle=\max_{1\leq j\leq n}\sum_{i=1}^{m}|a_{ij}|\quad (Maximum absolute column sum)
‖𝐀‖∞\displaystyle\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\infty} =max⁡∑j=1n1≤i≤m⁡|ai​j|\displaystyle=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|a_{ij}|\quad (Maximum absolute row sum)
‖𝐀‖max\displaystyle\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\max} =maxi,j⁡|ai​j|\displaystyle=\max_{i,j}|a_{ij}|\quad (Element-wise maximum, not a submultiplicative norm)
Definition 2 (Vectorization and Element-wise Operations).

Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} be a matrix and 𝐯\mathbf{v} be a vector.

  • •

    vecr​(𝐀)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A}) denotes the row-wise vectorization of matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}.

  • •

    𝐀∘α\mathbf{A}^{\circ\alpha} denotes the element-wise α\alpha-power of matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A}, i.e., (𝐀∘α)i​j=(𝐀i​j)α(\mathbf{A}^{\circ\alpha})_{ij}=(\mathbf{A}_{ij})^{\alpha}.

  • •

    diag​(𝐯)\textit{diag}(\mathbf{v}) creates a diagonal matrix with vector 𝐯\mathbf{v} on its main diagonal.

Property 1 (Relation between vec\mathrm{vec} and vecr\mathrm{vec}_{r}).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. The row-wise vectorization operator vecr\mathrm{vec}_{r} and the standard column-wise vectorization operator vec\mathrm{vec} are related by the transpose:

vecr​(𝐀)=vec⁡(𝐀⊤)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A})=\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{\top})
Definition 3 (Commutation Matrix).

The commutation matrix 𝐊m,n∈ℝm​n×m​n\mathbf{K}_{m,n}\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times mn} is the unique matrix such that for any matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} the following holds

𝐊m,n​vec​(𝐀)=vec⁡(𝐀⊤)\mathbf{K}_{m,n}\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A})=\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{\top})

Using Property 1, we immediately have the relationship:

vecr​(𝐀)=𝐊m,n​vec​(𝐀)andvec⁡(𝐀)=𝐊n,m​vecr​(𝐀)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{K}_{m,n}\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A})\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{K}_{n,m}\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A})

since 𝐊n,m​𝐊m,n=𝐈m​n\mathbf{K}_{n,m}\mathbf{K}_{m,n}=\mathbf{I}_{mn}.

From [38] we utilize the property

Property 2 (Row-wise vectorization of matrix product).

Let 𝐗,𝐀,𝐁\mathbf{X},\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B} be matrices with appropriate dimensions, then

vecr​(𝐀𝐗𝐁)=(𝐀⊗𝐁⊤)​vecr​(𝐗)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B})=(\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}^{\top})\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{X})
Property 3 (Row-wise vectorization of Hadamard product).

Let 𝐀,𝐁∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. Then

vecr​(𝐀∘𝐁)=diag​(vecr​(𝐀))​vecr​(𝐁)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A}\circ\mathbf{B})=\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A}))\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{B})

where ∘\circ denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product. This result follows directly from [38], where the similar result was obtained for column-wise vectorization.

Proposition 1 (Identification Theorem for Row-wise Vectorization).

Let 𝐅:ℝm×n→ℝp,q\mathbf{F}:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{p,q} be a differentiable matrix-valued function of a matrix 𝐗∈ℝm×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. If the differential of 𝐅\mathbf{F} can be written as

d​vecr​(𝐅⁡(𝐗))=𝐉⋅d​vecr​(𝐗)d\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}))=\mathbf{J}\cdot d\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{X})

for some matrix 𝐉∈ℝp​q×m​n\mathbf{J}\in\mathbb{R}^{pq\times mn} that does not depend on d​𝐗d\mathbf{X}. Then 𝐉\mathbf{J} is the Jacobian matrix of the transformation from 𝐗\mathbf{X} to 𝐅⁡(𝐗)\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) with respect to row-wise vectorization. We denote this as:

∂𝐅⁡(𝐗)∂𝐗:=∂vecr​(𝐅​(𝐗))∂(vecr​(𝐗))⊤=𝐉\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}:=\frac{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}))}{\partial(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{X}))^{\top}}=\mathbf{J}

This is the vecr\mathrm{vec}_{r} analogue of the fundamental Identification Theorem from [38] for column-wise vectorization.

Property 4 (Element-wise division).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be a matrix and 𝐛∈ℝm×1\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 1} be a vector. Then for matrix 𝐂∈∈ℝm×n\mathbf{C}\in{\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}}, where ci,j=ai,jbic_{i,j}=\frac{a_{i,j}}{b_{i}} is fulfilled that

𝐂=diag−1​(𝐛)​𝐀\mathbf{C}=\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathbf{b})\mathbf{A}
Proposition 2 (Spectral norm of 𝟏L×L\mathbf{1}_{L\times L} matrix).

Let 𝐀=𝟏L×L\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{1}_{L\times L} (a matrix full of 1). Then its spectral norm is

‖𝐀‖2=L\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}=L
Proof.

Using basic Linear Algebra properties, we obtain tr⁡(𝐀)=L\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{A})=L and rank⁡(𝐀)=1=dim⁡(Im⁡(𝐗))\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{A})=1=\mathrm{dim}(\mathrm{Im}(\mathbf{X})). Therefore, using dim⁡(Im⁡(𝐗))+dim⁡(Ker⁡(𝐗))=L\mathrm{dim}(\mathrm{Im}(\mathbf{X}))+\mathrm{dim}(\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf{X}))=L, we get dim⁡(Ker⁡(𝐗))=L−1\mathrm{dim}(\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf{X}))=L-1. Thus, for i∈{2,…​L}i\in\{2,\dots L\} we get λi=0\lambda_{i}=0 and for λ1=L\lambda_{1}=L. Then, the only non-null singular value of the matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} is L2=L\sqrt{L^{2}}=L. Thus, we obtain that ‖𝐀‖2=L\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}=L, according to Definition 1. ∎

B.2 Matrix-valued functions derivative properties

Next, we introduce the properties for calculating the matrix-valued function derivative.

Property 5 (Matrix-Product derivative).

Let 𝐗,𝐀,𝐁\mathbf{X},\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B} be matrices with appropriate dimensions, then

∂𝐀𝐗𝐁∂𝐗=𝐀⊗𝐁⊤\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}^{\top}

where 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} have no dependence on 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

Detailed proof of this statement can be found in [39].

Property 6 (Kronecker-Product derivative).

Let 𝐗∈ℝn×q\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q} and 𝐘∈ℝp×r\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r}. Then

∂(𝐗⊗𝐘)∂𝐗=(𝐈n⊗𝐊p,q⊗𝐈r)​(𝐈n​q⊗vecr​𝐘),\frac{\partial(\mathbf{X}\otimes\mathbf{Y})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=(\mathbf{I}_{n}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{p,q}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{r})\left(\mathbf{I}_{nq}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{Y}\right),

and analogously

∂(𝐗⊗𝐘)∂𝐘=(𝐈n⊗𝐊p,q⊗𝐈r)​(vecr​𝐗⊗𝐈p​r).\frac{\partial(\mathbf{X}\otimes\mathbf{Y})}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}=(\mathbf{I}_{n}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{p,q}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{r})\left(\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{X}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{pr}\right).

The detailed proof is in [12].

From the properties above, we derive calculations for special cases which we use in this paper.

Proposition 3 (Matrix-valued functions multiplication derivative).

Let 𝐀⁡(𝐗)∈ℝp×r\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r} and 𝐁⁡(𝐗)∈ℝr×q\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times q} be matrix-valued functions of the matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X}, then

∂𝐀⁡(𝐗)​𝐁​(𝐗)∂𝐗=(𝐀⊗𝐈q)​∂𝐁∂𝐗+(𝐈p⊗𝐁⊤)​∂𝐀∂𝐗\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\left(\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{q}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{p}\otimes\mathbf{B}^{\top}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}
Proof.

First, we apply a classic chain-rule for calculation a derivative of a complicated function and then combine it with Property 5

∂𝐀⁡(𝐗)​𝐁​(𝐗)∂𝐗\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}} =∂𝐀𝐁∂𝐁​∂𝐁∂𝐗+∂𝐀𝐁∂𝐀​∂𝐀∂𝐗=∂𝐀𝐁𝐈q∂𝐁​∂𝐁∂𝐗+∂𝐈p​𝐀𝐁∂𝐀​∂𝐀∂𝐗=\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{B}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{I}_{q}}{\partial\mathbf{B}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{I}_{p}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=
=(𝐀⊗𝐈q)​∂𝐁∂𝐗+(𝐈p⊗𝐁⊤)​∂𝐀∂𝐗\displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{q}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{p}\otimes\mathbf{B}^{\top}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

∎

Proposition 4 (Matrix-valued functions Kronecker product derivative).

Let 𝐀⁡(𝐗)∈ℝn×q\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q} and 𝐁⁡(𝐗)∈ℝp×r\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r} be matrix-valued functions of the matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X}, then

∂𝐀⁡(𝐗)⊗𝐁⁡(𝐗)∂𝐗=(𝐈n⊗𝐊p,q⊗𝐈r)​((vecr​𝐀⊗𝐈p​r)​∂𝐁∂𝐗+(𝐈n​q⊗vecr​𝐁)​∂𝐀∂𝐗)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{X})\otimes\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=(\mathbf{I}_{n}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{p,q}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{r})\left(\left(\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{pr}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{nq}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{B}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\right)
Proof.

First, we apply a classic chain rule for calculating the derivative of a complicated function and then combine it with Property 6

∂𝐀⁡(𝐗)⊗𝐁⁡(𝐗)∂𝐗\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{X})\otimes\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}} =∂𝐀⊗𝐁∂𝐁​∂𝐁∂𝐗+∂𝐀⊗𝐁∂𝐀​∂𝐀∂𝐗=\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{B}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=
=(𝐈n⊗𝐊p,q⊗𝐈r)​(vecr​𝐀⊗𝐈p​r)​∂𝐁∂𝐗+(𝐈n⊗𝐊p,q⊗𝐈r)​(𝐈n​q⊗vecr​𝐁)​∂𝐀∂𝐗=\displaystyle=(\mathbf{I}_{n}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{p,q}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{r})\left(\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{pr}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+(\mathbf{I}_{n}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{p,q}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{r})\left(\mathbf{I}_{nq}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{B}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=
=(𝐈n⊗𝐊p,q⊗𝐈r)​((vecr​𝐀⊗𝐈p​r)​∂𝐁∂𝐗+(𝐈n​q⊗vecr​𝐁)​∂𝐀∂𝐗)\displaystyle=(\mathbf{I}_{n}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{p,q}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{r})\left(\left(\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{pr}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{nq}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{B}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\right)

∎

Next, we develop the operations that we introduced above and derive calculations using vecr\mathrm{\text{vec}}_{r} notation as we do in this paper.

Proposition 5 (Derivative of the invert matrix).

For an invertible square matrix 𝐃∈ℝn×n\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, the derivative of its inverse is

∂𝐃−1∂𝐃=−𝐃−1⊗𝐃−⁣⊤.\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}^{-1}}{\partial\mathbf{D}}=-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{D}^{-\top}.
Proof.

This is a standard result in matrix calculus. The differential identity

d⁡(𝐃−1)=−𝐃−1​(d​𝐃)​𝐃−1d(\mathbf{D}^{-1})=-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\,(d\mathbf{D})\,\mathbf{D}^{-1}

appears in [40] and in [38]. Applying the vecr\mathrm{vec}_{r} operator and using the property 2 yields

vecr(−𝐃−1(d𝐃)𝐃−1)=(−𝐃−1⊗𝐃−⁣⊤)vecr(d𝐃)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\,(d\mathbf{D})\,\mathbf{D}^{-1})=(-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{D}^{-\top})\mathrm{vec}_{r}(d\mathbf{D})

By the definition and the identification theorem from Property 1 we obtain

vecr​(d​𝐃−1)=∂vecr​𝐃−1∂vecr​𝐃​vecr​(d​𝐃)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(d\mathbf{D}^{-1})=\frac{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{D}^{-1}}{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{D}}\mathrm{vec}_{r}(d\mathbf{D})

Comparing two results we get ∂vecr​𝐃−1∂vecr​𝐃=(−𝐃−1⊗𝐃−⁣⊤)\frac{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{D}^{-1}}{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}\mathbf{D}}=(-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{D}^{-\top})

∎

Proposition 6 (Derivative of diag⁡(⋅)\mathrm{diag}(\cdot)).

For 𝐯∈ℝL×1\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times 1}, the derivative of the diagonalization map is

∂diag⁡(𝐯)∂𝐯=(𝐞1⊗𝐞1…𝐞L⊗𝐞L),\frac{\partial\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{v})}{\partial\mathbf{v}}=\big(\mathbf{e}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{1}\quad\dots\quad\mathbf{e}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{L}\big),

where 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} are the standard basis vectors in ℝL\mathbb{R}^{L}.

Proof.

By Definition 2, diag⁡(𝐯)\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{v}) places entry viv_{i} at position (i,i)(i,i) of the resulting diagonal matrix.

The derivative of diag⁡(𝐯)\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{v}) w.r.t. viv_{i} is the elementary matrix 𝐄i​i=𝐞i​𝐞i⊤\mathbf{E}_{ii}=\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top} that has one in position (i,i)(i,i) and zeros elsewhere.

Applying the row-wise vectorization operator, we obtain

vecr​(𝐄i,i)=𝐞i⊗𝐞i\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{E}_{i,i})=\mathbf{e}_{i}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{i}

by the standard Kronecker–vec identity 2.

Stacking across i=1,…,Li=1,\dots,L, the Jacobian becomes

∂diag⁡(𝐯)∂𝐯=(𝐞1⊗𝐞1…𝐞L⊗𝐞L),\frac{\partial\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{v})}{\partial\mathbf{v}}=\big(\mathbf{e}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{1}\quad\dots\quad\mathbf{e}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{L}\big),

∎

Proposition 7 (Derivative of the Hadamard square).

For a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the derivative of the elementwise square is

∂𝐀∘2∂𝐀=2⋅diag⁡(vecr​(𝐀)).\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}^{\circ 2}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}=2\cdot\mathrm{diag}\!\big(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A})\big).
Proof.

By Definition 2, (𝐀∘2)​i​j=(𝐀​i​j)2(\mathbf{A}^{\circ 2}){ij}=(\mathbf{A}{ij})^{2}. Differentiating elementwise gives d⁡(𝐀∘2)=2​𝐀∘d​𝐀d(\mathbf{A}^{\circ 2})=2\mathbf{A}\circ d\mathbf{A}. Applying the vecr\mathrm{vec}_{r} operator and using Property 3, we obtain

vecr​(d⁡(𝐀∘2))=2​diag​(vecr​(𝐀))​vecr​(d​𝐀)\mathrm{vec}_{r}(d(\mathbf{A}^{\circ 2}))=2\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A}))\mathrm{vec}_{r}(d\mathbf{A})

By the identification theorem from Property 1, this implies

∂𝐀∘2∂𝐀=∂vecr​(𝐀∘2)∂vecr​(𝐀)=2⋅diag⁡(vecr​(𝐀))\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}^{\circ 2}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}=\frac{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A}^{\circ 2})}{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A})}=2\cdot\mathrm{diag}\!\big(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A})\big)

which establishes the result. ∎

Proposition 8 (Derivative of the Hadamard root).

For 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with positive entries, the derivative of the elementwise square root is

∂𝐀∘12∂𝐀=12​diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐀)).\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{diag}^{-1}\!\big(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{A})\big).
Proof.

Similarly to the proof of Proposition 7, we obtain d(𝐀∘1/2)=12𝐀∘−1/2∘d𝐀d(\mathbf{A}^{\circ 1/2})=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{A}^{\circ-1/2}\circ d\mathbf{A} Thus, writing in vectorized form gives

∂𝐀∘12∂𝐀=∂vecr​(𝐀∘12)∂vecr​(𝐀)=12​diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐀)).\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}=\frac{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}})}{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{A})}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{diag}^{-1}\!\big(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{A})\big).

∎

Proposition 9 (Transposed Matrix derivative).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, then the following holds:

∂𝐀⊤∂𝐀=𝐊n,m\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}^{\top}}{\partial\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{K}_{n,m}
Proof.

Combining a similar property from [38] for column-wise vectorization with the column-row connection rule 1 and 3 we obtain the theorem statement. ∎

B.3 Matrix norm properties

Similarly to [40] we introduce a matrix norms table comparison.

Property 7 (Matrix norm inequalities).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. Then the following inequalities hold between different matrix norms:

‖𝐀‖max\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\max} ‖𝐀‖1\|\mathbf{A}\|_{1} ‖𝐀‖∞\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\infty} ‖𝐀‖2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2} ‖𝐀‖F\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F}
‖𝐀‖max\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\max} 1 1 1 1
‖𝐀‖1\|\mathbf{A}\|_{1} mm mm m\sqrt{m} m\sqrt{m}
‖𝐀‖∞\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\infty} nn nn n\sqrt{n} n\sqrt{n}
‖𝐀‖2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2} m​n\sqrt{mn} n\sqrt{n} m\sqrt{m} 1
‖𝐀‖F\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F} m​n\sqrt{mn} n\sqrt{n} m\sqrt{m} d\sqrt{d}

where d=rank⁡(𝐀)d=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}). The table should be read as: for any two norms ∥⋅∥X\|\cdot\|_{X} and ∥⋅∥Y\|\cdot\|_{Y},

‖𝐀‖X≤c⋅‖𝐀‖Y\|\mathbf{A}\|_{X}\leq c\cdot\|\mathbf{A}\|_{Y}

where cc is the constant found at the intersection of row XX and column YY.

Property 8 (Matrix sum norm).

Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} be matrices from ℝm×n\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, then

‖𝐀+𝐁‖2≤‖𝐀‖2+‖𝐁‖2\|\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}+\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2} (11)
Property 9 (Kronecker product norm).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and 𝐁∈ℝp×q\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}, then the following holds

‖𝐀⊗𝐁‖2=‖𝐀‖2​‖𝐁‖2\|\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2}
Property 10 (Matrix product norm).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and 𝐁∈ℝn×q\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}, then the following holds

‖𝐀𝐁‖2≤‖𝐀‖2​‖𝐁‖2\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2}

The properties above can be found in [38].

Property 11 (Block-matrix norm inequality).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be a block-matrix, each block of which is a matrix 𝐁i,j\mathbf{B}_{i,j}, thus the following holds

‖𝐀‖2≤m​n​maxi,j​‖𝐁i,j‖2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{mn}\max\limits_{i,j}\|\mathbf{B}_{i,j}\|_{2}

Note, if matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} is block-diagonal, then the strict equality holds ‖𝐀‖2=maxi⁡‖𝐁i,i‖2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}=\max\limits_{i}\|\mathbf{B}_{i,i}\|_{2}.

Property 12 (Transposed matrix norm).

Let 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, then

‖𝐀‖2=‖𝐀⊤‖2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{A}^{\top}\|_{2}

C.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

From Lemma A.3 [14] and using Properties 10 and 9

‖∂𝐀∂𝐓‖2=1L​‖𝐈L‖2​‖𝐈L−1L​𝟏L×L‖2≤1L\displaystyle\|\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{T}}\|_{2}=\frac{1}{L}\|\mathbf{I}_{L}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{I}_{L}-\frac{1}{L}\mathbf{1}_{L\times L}\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{L}

Here we used that 1L​𝟏L×L\frac{1}{L}\mathbf{1}_{L\times L} is a projection matrix, therefore 𝐈L−1L​𝟏L×L\mathbf{I}_{L}-\frac{1}{L}\mathbf{1}_{L\times L} is a projection matrix and it’s norm is ‖𝐈L−1L​𝟏L×L‖2≤1\|\mathbf{I}_{L}-\frac{1}{L}\mathbf{1}_{L\times L}\|_{2}\leq 1.

Next we estimate the 𝐙1\mathbf{Z}_{1} norm, utilizing the same Properties 10 and 9

where we used Property 12 for ‖𝐗‖2=‖𝐗⊤‖2\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\|_{2}.

Now we calculate estimations for the outer-product Hessian part.

But before that we estimate ‖𝐀‖2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}. This block itself is a row-wise softmax matrix. Thus, each element 𝐀i,j≤1\mathbf{A}_{i,j}\leq 1. Next we use Property 7 and obtain ‖𝐀‖max≤‖𝐀‖2≤L​L​‖𝐀‖max=L​‖𝐀‖m​a​x≤L\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\max}\leq\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{LL}\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\max}=L\|\mathbf{A}\|_{max}\leq L. Therefore, the ‖𝐌1‖2=‖𝐀𝐗‖2≤L​‖𝐗‖2\|\mathbf{M}_{1}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}\leq L\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}.

Let 𝐗∈ℝL×dV\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{V}}. Define

where 𝐏⁡(𝐗)=𝐃−1, where ​𝐃=diag​(σ⁡(𝐗))\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{D}^{-1},\text{ where }\mathbf{D}=\textit{diag}(\sigma(\mathbf{X})) and 𝐌⁡(𝐗)=(𝐗−μ⁡(𝐗)​𝟏dV⊤)\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{X})=(\mathbf{X}-\mu(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{1}^{\top}_{d_{V}}) according to Property 4.

Therefore, by utilizing Properties 7, 8 and 5 we can find

∂σ⁡(𝐗)∂𝐗=1dV​∂τ∘12∂τ​∂τ∂𝐐​∂𝐐∂𝐗,\frac{\partial\sigma(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{V}}}\frac{\partial\tau^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}}{\partial\tau}\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial\mathbf{Q}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{Q}}{\partial{\mathbf{X}}},

Here τ=𝐐⋅𝟏L\tau=\mathbf{Q}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{L} and 𝐐=𝐌∘2\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{M}^{\circ{2}}. Thus, we can continue calculations and obtain

=1dV​12​diag−1​(vecr∘12​(τ))​(𝐈L⊗𝟏dVT)​2⋅diag​(vecr​(𝐌))​∂𝐌∂𝐗=\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{V}}}\frac{1}{2}\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\tau))(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{1}^{T}_{d_{V}})2\cdot\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M}))\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=
=1dV​diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐌∘2⋅𝟏dV))⋅(𝐈L⊗𝟏dVT)⋅diag​(vecr​(𝐌))​∂𝐌∂𝐗\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{V}}}\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{M}^{\circ{2}}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d_{V}}))\cdot(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{1}^{T}_{d_{V}})\cdot\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M}))\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

Therefore, by applying 5 and 6 for the first and second multiplier, we obtain

(diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐌∘2⋅𝟏dV))⋅(𝐈L⊗𝟏dVT)⋅diag​(vecr​(𝐌))​∂𝐌∂𝐗)\displaystyle\left(\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{M}^{\circ{2}}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d_{V}}))\cdot(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{1}^{T}_{d_{V}})\cdot\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M}))\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\right)

C.3 Proof of Theorem 3

Proof.

Now, we calculate the second derivative ∂2LayerNorm∂𝐗2\frac{\partial^{2}\text{LayerNorm}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}}. Using the matrix product derivative property 5, we obtain:

∂2LayerNorm∂𝐗2\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\text{LayerNorm}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}} =((𝐏⁡(𝐗)⊗𝐈dV)⊗𝐈L​dV)​∂2𝐌∂𝐗2+(𝐈L​dV⊗(∂𝐌∂𝐗)⊤)​∂(𝐏⁡(𝐗)⊗𝐈dV)∂𝐗+\displaystyle=\left((\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{X})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\right)\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes(\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}})^{\top}\right)\frac{\partial(\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{X})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+
+((𝐈L⊗𝐌⊤)⊗𝐈L​dV)​∂2𝐏∂𝐗2+(𝐈L​dV⊗(∂𝐏∂𝐗)⊤)​∂(𝐈L⊗𝐌⊤)∂𝐗\displaystyle+\left((\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{M}^{\top})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\right)\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes(\frac{\partial\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}})^{\top}\right)\frac{\partial(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{M}^{\top})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

Here, we have 𝐏∈ℝL×L\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L}, 𝐌∈ℝL×dV\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{V}}, ∂𝐌∂𝐗∈ℝL​dV×L​dV\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times Ld_{V}}, ∂𝐏∂𝐗∈ℝL2×L​dV\frac{\partial\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times Ld_{V}}

Next, we can easily obtain, using Properties 6, 9:

∂2𝐌∂𝐗2\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}} =0\displaystyle=0
∂(𝐏⁡(𝐗)⊗𝐈dV)∂𝐗\displaystyle\frac{\partial(\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{X})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})}{\partial\mathbf{X}} =∂(𝐏⊗𝐈L)∂𝐏​∂𝐏∂𝐗=(𝐈L⊗𝐊L,L⊗𝐈L)​(𝐈L2⊗vecr​(𝐈L))​∂𝐏∂𝐗\displaystyle=\frac{\partial(\mathbf{P}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{L})}{\partial\mathbf{P}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{L,L}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{L}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{L^{2}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{L})\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}
∂(𝐈L⊗𝐌⊤)∂𝐗\displaystyle\frac{\partial(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{M}^{\top})}{\partial\mathbf{X}} =∂(𝐈L⊗𝐌⊤)∂𝐌⊤​∂𝐌⊤∂𝐌​∂𝐌∂𝐗=(𝐈L⊗𝐊dV,L⊗𝐈L)​(vecr​(𝐈L)⊗𝐈L​dV)​𝐊dV,L​∂𝐌∂𝐗\displaystyle=\frac{\partial(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{M}^{\top})}{\partial\mathbf{M}^{\top}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}^{\top}}{\partial\mathbf{M}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{V},L}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{L}\right)\left(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{L})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\right)\mathbf{K}_{d_{V},L}\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

Now, we analyze the second-order derivative of the 𝐏\mathbf{P} matrix. To derive correct calculations we need to write the dimensions of each multiplier in the calculated first derivative out. Matrix 𝐃\mathbf{D} is a diag​(σ​(𝐗))\textit{diag}(\sigma(\mathbf{X})), the size of vector σ⁡(𝐗)\sigma(\mathbf{X}) is L×1L\times 1, therefore, 𝐃∈ℝL×L\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L} and the part (−𝐃−1⊗𝐃−⁣⊤)∈ℝL2×L2\left(-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{D}^{-\top}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times L^{2}}. Next, we note that the size of each basis vector 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} is L×1L\times 1, thus we obtain 𝐞i⊗𝐞i∈ℝL2×1\mathbf{e}_{i}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times 1} and (𝐞1⊗𝐞1…𝐞L⊗𝐞L)∈ℝL2×L\Big(\mathbf{e}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{1}\quad\dots\quad\mathbf{e}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{L}\Big)\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times L}. As we discussed earlier, 𝐌⁡(𝐗)∈ℝL×dV\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{V}}, then M⋅𝟏dV∈ℝL×1M\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d_{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times 1}, and we can derive the size of diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐌∘2⋅𝟏dV))\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{M}^{\circ{2}}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d_{V}})), which is L×LL\times L. The last one is ∂𝐌∂𝐗\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}, which we have already calculated, it’s size is L​dV×L​dVLd_{V}\times Ld_{V}. Therefore, the whole derivative ∂𝐏∂𝐗\frac{\partial\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}} is from ℝL2×L​dV\mathbb{R}^{L^{2}\times Ld_{V}}.

We start with ∂𝐏∂𝐗=1dV​𝐀1​(𝐗)⋅𝐁1​(𝐗)\frac{\partial\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{V}}}\mathbf{A}_{1}(\mathbf{X})\cdot\mathbf{B}_{1}(\mathbf{X}), where 𝐀1=(−𝐃−1⊗𝐃−⁣⊤)\mathbf{A}_{1}=\left(-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{D}^{-\top}\right) and 𝐁1\mathbf{B}_{1} is the other multiplier.

∂2𝐏∂𝐗2=1dV​∂𝐀1​(𝐗)⋅𝐁1​(𝐗)∂𝐗=1dV​(𝐀1⊗𝐈L​dV)​∂𝐁1∂𝐗+(𝐈L2⊗𝐁1⊤)​∂𝐀1∂𝐗\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{V}}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}_{1}(\mathbf{X})\cdot\mathbf{B}_{1}(\mathbf{X})}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{V}}}\left(\mathbf{A}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}_{1}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{L^{2}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{1}^{\top}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}_{1}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

+(vecr(−𝐃−𝟏)⊗𝐈L2)⋅∂𝐃−⁣⊤∂𝐗)\displaystyle+(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(-\mathbf{\mathbf{D}^{-1}})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{L^{2}})\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}^{-\top}}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\Big)

By using the transposed matrix and the invert matrix derivative properties 9, 5, we obtain: ∂−𝐃−𝟏∂𝐗=∂−𝐃−𝟏∂𝐃​∂𝐃∂𝐗=(𝐃−1⊗𝐃−⁣⊤)​∂𝐃∂𝐗\frac{\partial-\mathbf{\mathbf{D}^{-1}}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{\partial-\mathbf{\mathbf{D}^{-1}}}{\partial\mathbf{D}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\left(\mathbf{D}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{D}^{-\top}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial\mathbf{X}} and ∂𝐃−⁣⊤∂𝐗=∂𝐃−⁣⊤∂𝐃−1∂𝐃−𝟏∂𝐃∂𝐃∂𝐗=𝐊L,L(−𝐃−1⊗𝐃−⁣⊤)∂𝐃∂𝐗\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}^{-\top}}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}^{-\top}}}{\partial\mathbf{D}^{-1}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}^{-1}}}{\partial\mathbf{D}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{K}_{L,L}\left(-\mathbf{D}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{D}^{-\top}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}, where we the ∂𝐃∂𝐗\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}}}{\partial\mathbf{X}} as we calculated earlier, while computing the first LayerNorm’s derivative is ∂𝐃∂𝐗=(𝐞1⊗𝐞1…𝐞L⊗𝐞L)​(diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐌∘2⋅𝟏dV))⋅(𝐈L⊗𝟏dVT)⋅diag​(vecr​(𝐌))​∂𝐌∂𝐗)\frac{\partial\mathbf{\mathbf{D}}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\Big(\mathbf{e}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{1}\quad\dots\quad\mathbf{e}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{L}\Big)\left(\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{M}^{\circ{2}}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d_{V}}))\cdot(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{1}^{T}_{d_{V}})\cdot\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M}))\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\right)

And now we proceed to the calculations of the remaining part derivative.

We first assign new 𝐀2\mathbf{A}_{2} and 𝐁2\mathbf{B}_{2} for clear calculations. We have 𝐁1=(𝐞1⊗𝐞1…𝐞L⊗𝐞L)​(diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐌∘2⋅𝟏dV))⋅(𝐈L⊗𝟏dVT)⋅diag​(vecr​(𝐌))​∂𝐌∂𝐗)\mathbf{B}_{1}=\Big(\mathbf{e}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{1}\quad\dots\quad\mathbf{e}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{L}\Big)\left(\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{M}^{\circ{2}}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d_{V}}))\cdot(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{1}^{T}_{d_{V}})\cdot\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M}))\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\right) and we assign new 𝐀2\mathbf{A}_{2} and new 𝐁2\mathbf{B}_{2} as 𝐀2=diag−1​(vecr∘12​(𝐌∘2⋅𝟏dV))\mathbf{A}_{2}=\textit{diag}^{-1}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}^{\circ\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbf{M}^{\circ{2}}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d_{V}})), 𝐁2=(𝐈L⊗𝟏dVT)⋅diag​(vecr​(𝐌))​∂𝐌∂𝐗\mathbf{B}_{2}=(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{1}^{T}_{d_{V}})\cdot\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M}))\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}} and we denote 𝐄=(𝐞1⊗𝐞1…𝐞L⊗𝐞L)\mathbf{E}=\Big(\mathbf{e}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{1}\quad\dots\quad\mathbf{e}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{L}\Big). Thus, 𝐁1=𝐄𝐀2​𝐁2\mathbf{B}_{1}=\mathbf{E}\mathbf{A}_{2}\mathbf{B}_{2}

While 𝐄\mathbf{E} is a constant matrix we can apply the simplified matrix product derivative rule 3 and obtain

∂𝐁1∂𝐗\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}_{1}}{\partial\mathbf{X}} =∂𝐄𝐀2​𝐁2∂(𝐀2​𝐁2)​∂𝐀2​𝐁2∂𝐗=(𝐄⊗𝐈L​dV)​∂𝐀2​𝐁2∂𝐗\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}\mathbf{A}_{2}\mathbf{B}_{2}}{\partial(\mathbf{A}_{2}\mathbf{B}_{2})}\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}_{2}\mathbf{B}_{2}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\left(\mathbf{E}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}_{2}\mathbf{B}_{2}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

Now, we introduce the last 𝐀3\mathbf{A}_{3} and 𝐁3\mathbf{B}_{3} assignment. =(𝐉⊗𝐈L​dV)​((𝐀3⊗𝐈L​dV)​∂𝐁3∂𝐗+(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐁3⊤)​∂𝐀3∂𝐗)\displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{J}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\right)\left((\mathbf{A}_{3}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}})\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}_{3}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{3}^{\top})\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}_{3}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}\right)

Where both Jacobian matrices can be found easily ∂𝐀3∂𝐗=∂diag​(vecr​(𝐌))∂𝐗=∂diag​(𝐯)∂(𝐯)​∂vecr​(𝐌)∂𝐌​∂𝐌∂𝐗\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}_{3}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{\partial\textit{diag}(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M}))}{\partial\mathbf{X}}=\frac{\partial\textit{diag}(\mathbf{v})}{\partial(\mathbf{v})}\frac{\partial\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{M})}{\partial\mathbf{M}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{M}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

∂2𝐏∂𝐗2\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{P}}{\partial\mathbf{X}^{2}} =1dV​(𝐀1⊗𝐈L​dV)​∂𝐁1∂𝐗+(𝐈L2⊗𝐁1⊤)​∂𝐀1∂𝐗\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{V}}}\left(\mathbf{A}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}_{1}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{L^{2}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{1}^{\top}\right)\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}_{1}}{\partial\mathbf{X}}

The last step in the proof is simply combining all together and substituting all calculated derivatives into the LayerNorm’s Hessian.

That ends the proof. ∎

It’s worth noting that in our notation 𝐗∈RL×dV,𝐘∈RL×dV,𝐖1∈RdV×df​f,ReLU​(𝐘𝐖𝟏)∈RL×df​f,𝐖2∈Rdf​f×dV\mathbf{X}\in R^{L\times d_{V}},\mathbf{Y}\in R^{L\times d_{V}},\mathbf{W}_{1}\in R^{d_{V}\times d_{ff}},\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{Y\mathbf{W}_{1}})\in R^{L\times d_{ff}},\mathbf{W}_{2}\in R^{d_{ff}\times d_{V}}.

for ​i=2:\displaystyle\text{for }i=2: ∂𝐈L​σ​(𝐘𝐖1)​𝐖2​𝐈dV∂𝐖i=σ⁡(𝐘𝐖1)⊗𝐈dV\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbf{I}_{L}\sigma(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}

Theorem 10 (Detailed version of Theorem 5).

Let further

𝐃σ:=diag(vecr(𝟏{𝐘𝐖1>0}))∈ℝL​df​f×L​df​f\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}:=\mathrm{diag}\big(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{1}_{\{\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1}>0\}})\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{ff}\times Ld_{ff}}

from Lemma 1.

𝐉S​Y:=∂𝐒∂𝐘=(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ​(𝐈L⊗𝐖1⊤)+(𝐈L⊗𝐈dV)∈ℝL​dV×L​dV,\mathbf{J}_{SY}:=\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}=(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{1}^{\top})+(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times Ld_{V}},

calculated by Theorems 2–3.

Denote parameter sizes

n1=dV​df​f,n2=df​f​dV,nQ=nK=dV​dK,nV=dV2.n_{1}=d_{V}d_{ff},\quad n_{2}=d_{ff}d_{V},\quad n_{Q}=n_{K}=d_{V}d_{K},\quad n_{V}=d_{V}^{2}.

𝐆V:=∂𝐅∂𝐖V∈ℝL​dV×nV,𝐆Q:=∂𝐅∂𝐖Q∈ℝL​dV×nQ,𝐆K:=∂𝐅∂𝐖K∈ℝL​dV×nK.\mathbf{G}_{V}:=\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times n_{V}},\quad\mathbf{G}_{Q}:=\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{Q}}\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times n_{Q}},\quad\mathbf{G}_{K}:=\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{K}}\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times n_{K}}.

Then the Hessian blocks of the Transformer output 𝐙\mathbf{Z} w.r.t. parameters (𝐖i,𝐖j)(\mathbf{W}_{i},\mathbf{W}_{j}) are

𝐇tr(i,j):=∂2𝐙∂𝐖i​∂𝐖j=(𝐉Z⊗𝐈ni)​𝝃i​j+(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐁i⊤)​𝐇Z​𝐁j\boxed{\;\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}:=\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}=\left(\mathbf{J}_{Z}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{i}}\right)\bm{\xi}_{ij}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{i}^{\top}\right)\mathbf{H}_{Z}\mathbf{B}_{j}\;} (12)

with

The second Jacobians 𝛏i​j\bm{\xi}_{ij} for all pairs (i,j)(i,j) are given almost everywhere by:

1) Pure-FFN pairs:

𝝃11=𝟎(L​dV⋅n1)×n1,𝝃22=𝟎(L​dV⋅n2)×n2,\bm{\xi}_{11}=\mathbf{0}_{(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{1})\times n_{1}},\qquad\bm{\xi}_{22}=\mathbf{0}_{(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{2})\times n_{2}},
𝝃12=(𝐈L⊗𝐊dV,df​f⊗𝐈dV)​(𝐈L​df​f⊗vecr​(𝐈dV))​(𝐃σ​(𝐘⊗𝐈df​f)),\bm{\xi}_{12}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{V},d_{ff}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{ff}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})\right)\left(\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}\,(\mathbf{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})\right),
𝝃21=(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ​(𝐈L⊗𝐊df​f,dV⊗𝐈df​f)​(𝐈L​dV⊗vecr​(𝐈df​f)).\bm{\xi}_{21}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top}\right)\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{ff},d_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})\right).

Both 𝛏12\bm{\xi}_{12} and 𝛏21\bm{\xi}_{21} are (L​dV⋅n1)×n2(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{1})\times n_{2} and (L​dV⋅n2)×n1(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{2})\times n_{1} respectively. They agree almost everywhere when pre- and post-composed in equation 6 (see symmetry discussion).

2) FFN–attention pairs (k∈{K,Q,V}k\in\{K,Q,V\}):

𝝃1​k=((𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ⊗𝐈nk)​(𝐈L⊗𝐊df​f,dV⊗𝐈df​f)​(𝐈L​dV⊗vecr​(𝐈df​f))​(𝐉Y​𝐆k),\bm{\xi}_{1k}=\left((\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{ff},d_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})\right)\left(\mathbf{J}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{k}\right),
𝝃2​k=(𝐈L⊗𝐊dV,df​f⊗𝐈dV)​(𝐈L​df​f⊗vecr​(𝐈dV))​(𝐃σ​(𝐈L⊗𝐖1⊤)​𝐉Y​𝐆k).\bm{\xi}_{2k}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{V},d_{ff}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{ff}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})\right)\left(\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{1}^{\top})\,\mathbf{J}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{k}\right).

𝝃k​ℓ=(𝐉S​Y⊗𝐈nk)​[(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐆k⊤)​(𝐇Y​𝐆ℓ)+(𝐉Y⊗𝐈nk)​𝚽k​ℓ],\bm{\xi}_{k\ell}=\left(\mathbf{J}_{SY}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}}\right)\left[\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{G}_{k}^{\top}\right)\left(\mathbf{H}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{\ell}\right)+\left(\mathbf{J}_{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}}\right)\bm{\Phi}_{k\ell}\right],

where 𝚽k​ℓ:=∂𝐆k∂𝐖ℓ∈ℝ(L​dV⋅nk)×nℓ\bm{\Phi}_{k\ell}:=\frac{\partial\mathbf{G}_{k}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\ell}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{k})\times n_{\ell}} are second derivatives of the attention map 𝐅\mathbf{F} w.r.t. its weights. The exact values are calculated in Lemma 2 basing on the results from [12]. All matrices are dimensionally consistent: 𝛏k​ℓ∈ℝ(L​dV⋅nk)×nℓ\bm{\xi}_{k\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{k})\times n_{\ell}}.

Finally, the Hessian block equation 6 has size 𝐇tr(i,j)∈ℝ(L​dV⋅ni)×nj\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{i})\times n_{j}}.

Moreover, all mixed blocks are symmetric almost everywhere:

𝐇tr(i,j)=𝐇tr(j,i)a.e.,\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(j,i)}\quad\text{a.e.},

because (i) the only nonlinearities with potentially nonzero second differential are LayerNorm (handled by 𝐇Z,𝐇Y\mathbf{H}_{Z},\mathbf{H}_{Y} which are symmetric by construction in Theorem 3) and ReLU (whose Hessian is zero a.e., Lemma 1), and (ii) all remaining mappings are multilinear in the parameters; thus, by repeated applications of Proposition 3 and Proposition 6, the mixed-partials commute almost everywhere.

Proof.

We differentiate the Jacobian from Theorem 4 using Proposition 3 (matrix-product derivative), Proposition 6 (Kronecker-product derivative), Proposition 9, the Identification Theorem 1, and Lemma 1.

Step 1. For any i∈{1,2,K,Q,V}i\in\{1,2,K,Q,V\} we have

∂𝐙∂𝐖i=𝐉Z​𝐁i,𝐉Z∈ℝL​dV×L​dV,\frac{\partial\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}}\;=\;\mathbf{J}_{Z}\,\mathbf{B}_{i},\qquad\mathbf{J}_{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times Ld_{V}},

𝐁1=(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ​(𝐘⊗𝐈df​f)∈ℝL​dV×n1,𝐁2=σ⁡(𝐘𝐖1)⊗𝐈dV∈ℝL​dV×n2,\mathbf{B}_{1}=(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})\,\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}\,(\mathbf{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times n_{1}},\quad\mathbf{B}_{2}=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times n_{2}},

with 𝐉S​Y=∂𝐒∂𝐘=(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ​(𝐈L⊗𝐖1⊤)+(𝐈L⊗𝐈dV)∈ℝL​dV×L​dV\mathbf{J}_{SY}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}=(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{1}^{\top})+(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times Ld_{V}}, 𝐉Y∈ℝL​dV×L​dV\mathbf{J}_{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{Ld_{V}\times Ld_{V}} and 𝐆k\mathbf{G}_{k} as in Theorem 4. ∂2𝐙∂𝐖i​∂𝐖j=(𝐉Z⊗𝐈ni)​𝝃i​j+(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐁i⊤)​𝐇Z​𝐁j,𝝃i​j:=∂𝐁i∂𝐖j∈ℝ(L​dV⋅ni)×nj.\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{Z}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{i}\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}=\left(\mathbf{J}_{Z}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{i}}\right)\bm{\xi}_{ij}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{i}^{\top}\right)\mathbf{H}_{Z}\mathbf{B}_{j},\qquad\bm{\xi}_{ij}:=\frac{\partial\,\mathbf{B}_{i}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{j}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(Ld_{V}\cdot n_{i})\times n_{j}}.

∂𝐁2∂𝐖1=(𝐈L⊗𝐊dV,df​f⊗𝐈dV)​(𝐈L​df​f⊗vecr​(𝐈dV))​∂vecr​(σ⁡(𝐘𝐖1))∂𝐖1.\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}_{2}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{1}}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{V},d_{ff}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{ff}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})\right)\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\sigma(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1}))}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{1}}.

- (2,1)(2,1): Differentiate 𝐁1=(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ​(𝐘⊗𝐈df​f)\mathbf{B}_{1}=(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})\,\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}\,(\mathbf{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}) w.r.t. 𝐖2\mathbf{W}_{2}. ∂vecr​(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)∂𝐖2=(𝐈L⊗𝐊dV,L⊗𝐈df​f)​(vecr​(𝐈L)⊗𝐈dV​df​f)​𝐊df​f,dV.\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{2}}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{V},L}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}\right)\left(\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{L})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}d_{ff}}\right)\mathbf{K}_{d_{ff},d_{V}}.

Collecting,

𝝃21=(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ​(𝐈L⊗𝐊df​f,dV⊗𝐈df​f)​(𝐈L​dV⊗vecr​(𝐈df​f)),\bm{\xi}_{21}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top}\right)\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{ff},d_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})\right),

which is the stated form. (Both 𝝃12\bm{\xi}_{12} and 𝝃21\bm{\xi}_{21} are consistent and coincide almost everywhere when inserted into equation 6; see symmetry below.)

3.2) FFN–attention pairs (1,k)(1,k), (2,k)(2,k) with k∈{K,Q,V}k\in\{K,Q,V\}. - (1,k)(1,k): 𝐁1=(𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ​(𝐘⊗𝐈df​f)\mathbf{B}_{1}=(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}). Using Proposition 3 (with the first factors constant a.e.), and the chain rule through 𝐘\mathbf{Y}:

∂vecr​(𝐘⊗𝐈df​f)∂𝐖k=(∂(𝐘⊗𝐈df​f)∂𝐘)​∂vecr​(𝐘)∂𝐖k.\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{k}}=\left(\frac{\partial(\mathbf{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}\right)\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{Y})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{k}}.

By Proposition 6 with 𝐗=𝐘\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{Y} and 𝐘=𝐈df​f\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}},

∂(𝐘⊗𝐈df​f)∂𝐘=(𝐈L⊗𝐊df​f,dV⊗𝐈df​f)​(𝐈L​dV⊗vecr​(𝐈df​f)).\frac{\partial(\mathbf{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{ff},d_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})\right).

Also ∂vecr​(𝐘)∂𝐖k=𝐉Y​𝐆k\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{Y})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{k}}=\mathbf{J}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{k} (Theorem 4 and Theorem 2). Therefore

𝝃1​k=((𝐈L⊗𝐖2⊤)​𝐃σ⊗𝐈nk)​(𝐈L⊗𝐊df​f,dV⊗𝐈df​f)​(𝐈L​dV⊗vecr​(𝐈df​f))​(𝐉Y​𝐆k).\bm{\xi}_{1k}=\left((\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{ff},d_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{ff}})\right)\left(\mathbf{J}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{k}\right).

- (2,k)(2,k): 𝐁2=σ⁡(𝐘𝐖1)⊗𝐈dV\mathbf{B}_{2}=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1})\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}. Differentiating the Kronecker product w.r.t. its first factor and applying the chain rule through 𝐘\mathbf{Y},

𝝃2​k=(𝐈L⊗𝐊dV,df​f⊗𝐈dV)​(𝐈L​df​f⊗vecr​(𝐈dV))​(𝐃σ​(𝐈L⊗𝐖1⊤)​𝐉Y​𝐆k),\bm{\xi}_{2k}=\left(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{K}_{d_{V},d_{ff}}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}\right)\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{ff}}\otimes\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}})\right)\left(\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{1}^{\top})\,\mathbf{J}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{k}\right),

where we used Property 5 to write ∂(𝐘𝐖1)∂𝐘=𝐈L⊗𝐖1⊤\frac{\partial(\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{W}_{1})}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{1}^{\top} and Lemma 1 for ∂σ⁡(⋅)∂(⋅)=𝐃σ\frac{\partial\sigma(\cdot)}{\partial(\cdot)}=\mathbf{D}_{\sigma}.

3.3) Pure-attention pairs (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) with k,ℓ∈{K,Q,V}k,\ell\in\{K,Q,V\}. We start from 𝐁k=𝐉S​Y​𝐉Y​𝐆k\mathbf{B}_{k}=\mathbf{J}_{SY}\,\mathbf{J}_{Y}\,\mathbf{G}_{k}. Almost everywhere ∂𝐉S​Y∂𝐘=𝟎\frac{\partial\mathbf{J}_{SY}}{\partial\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{0} because 𝐃σ\mathbf{D}_{\sigma} is piecewise constant (Lemma 1). Therefore,

∂vecr​(𝐁k)∂𝐖ℓ=(𝐉S​Y⊗𝐈nk)​∂vecr​(𝐉Y​𝐆k)∂𝐖ℓ\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{B}_{k})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\ell}}=(\mathbf{J}_{SY}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}})\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{J}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{k})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\ell}}

by Proposition 3. Again by Proposition 3 with 𝐀⁡(⋅)=𝐉Y\mathbf{A}(\cdot)=\mathbf{J}_{Y} and 𝐁⁡(⋅)=𝐆k\mathbf{B}(\cdot)=\mathbf{G}_{k},

∂vecr​(𝐉Y​𝐆k)∂𝐖ℓ=(𝐉Y⊗𝐈nk)​𝚽k​ℓ+(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐆k⊤)​∂vecr​(𝐉Y)∂𝐖ℓ.\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{J}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{k})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\ell}}=(\mathbf{J}_{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}})\bm{\Phi}_{k\ell}+\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{G}_{k}^{\top}\right)\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{J}_{Y})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\ell}}.

By Theorem 3 and the Identification Theorem 1, ∂vecr​(𝐉Y)∂𝐖ℓ=𝐇Y​𝐆ℓ\frac{\partial\,\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{J}_{Y})}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\ell}}=\mathbf{H}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{\ell}. Thus

𝝃k​ℓ=(𝐉S​Y⊗𝐈nk)​[(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐆k⊤)​(𝐇Y​𝐆ℓ)+(𝐉Y⊗𝐈nk)​𝚽k​ℓ].\bm{\xi}_{k\ell}=\left(\mathbf{J}_{SY}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}}\right)\left[\left(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{G}_{k}^{\top}\right)\left(\mathbf{H}_{Y}\mathbf{G}_{\ell}\right)+\left(\mathbf{J}_{Y}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}}\right)\bm{\Phi}_{k\ell}\right].

It remains to specify 𝚽k​ℓ:=∂𝐆k∂𝐖ℓ\bm{\Phi}_{k\ell}:=\frac{\partial\mathbf{G}_{k}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\ell}}. Using the explicit 𝐆k\mathbf{G}_{k} from Theorem 4 and only Proposition 3, Proposition 6, and Proposition 9, we obtain the forms stated in the theorem. Under the uniform-attention simplification (so ∂𝐀∂𝐌\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{M}} is a constant matrix), 𝐆V\mathbf{G}_{V} does not depend on 𝐖Q,𝐖K,𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V}; 𝐆Q\mathbf{G}_{Q} does not depend on 𝐖Q\mathbf{W}_{Q}; 𝐆K\mathbf{G}_{K} does not depend on 𝐖K\mathbf{W}_{K}; hence 𝚽V​V=𝚽V​Q=𝚽V​K=𝚽Q​Q=𝚽K​K=𝟎\bm{\Phi}_{VV}=\bm{\Phi}_{VQ}=\bm{\Phi}_{VK}=\bm{\Phi}_{QQ}=\bm{\Phi}_{KK}=\mathbf{0}; and the remaining mixed terms are given by differentiating the Kronecker factors using Proposition 6 and the transpose dependence using Proposition 9, exactly as written.

Step 4: Symmetry of mixed partials. All nonlinearities that could obstruct symmetry are ReLU and LayerNorm. ReLU has zero Hessian almost everywhere (Lemma 1), so its contribution to second differentials vanishes a.e. LayerNorm Hessians 𝐇Z\mathbf{H}_{Z} and 𝐇Y\mathbf{H}_{Y} are the derivatives of Jacobians w.r.t. their inputs and enter symmetrically (Theorem 3). All remaining mappings are multilinear in parameters and matrices independent of (𝐖i,𝐖j)(\mathbf{W}_{i},\mathbf{W}_{j}); therefore, by repeated applications of Proposition 3 and Proposition 6, the mixed partials commute, giving 𝐇tr(i,j)=𝐇tr(j,i)\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(j,i)} almost everywhere.

This completes the proof. ∎

C.6 Proof of Theorem 6

Proof.

We start from the block formula equation 6:

𝐇tr(i,j)=(𝐉Z⊗𝐈ni)​𝝃i​j+(𝐈L​dV⊗𝐁i⊤)​𝐇Z​𝐁j.\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}=\big(\mathbf{J}_{Z}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{i}}\big)\,\bm{\xi}_{ij}+\big(\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{i}^{\top}\big)\,\mathbf{H}_{Z}\,\mathbf{B}_{j}.

Applying the matrix sum norm (Property 8) and the product norm (Property 10) together with the Kronecker product norm (Property 9) yields

‖𝐇tr(i,j)‖2≤‖𝐉Z⊗𝐈ni‖2​‖𝝃i​j‖2+‖𝐈L​dV⊗𝐁i⊤‖2​‖𝐇Z‖2​‖𝐁j‖2=‖𝐉Z‖2​‖𝝃i​j‖2+‖𝐁i‖2​‖𝐇Z‖2​‖𝐁j‖2,\big\|\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i,j)}\big\|_{2}\leq\big\|\mathbf{J}_{Z}\otimes\mathbf{I}_{n_{i}}\big\|_{2}\,\|\bm{\xi}_{ij}\|_{2}+\big\|\mathbf{I}_{Ld_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{i}^{\top}\big\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{H}_{Z}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{B}_{j}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{J}_{Z}\|_{2}\,\|\bm{\xi}_{ij}\|_{2}+\|\mathbf{B}_{i}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{H}_{Z}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{B}_{j}\|_{2},

establishing equation 8.

It remains to provide explicit operator-norm estimates for ‖𝐁i‖2\|\mathbf{B}_{i}\|_{2} and ‖𝝃i​j‖2\|\bm{\xi}_{ij}\|_{2} used inside equation 8. We rely on Properties 10, 9, 8, 7, 12, and the commutation properties (Definition 3). Throughout we use ‖𝐊m,n‖2=1\|\mathbf{K}_{m,n}\|_{2}=1 for commutation matrices, and the identities ‖vecr​(𝐈d)‖2=‖𝐈d‖F=d\|\mathrm{vec}_{r}(\mathbf{I}_{d})\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{I}_{d}\|_{F}=\sqrt{d} (Property 7) and ‖𝐈p‖2=1\|\mathbf{I}_{p}\|_{2}=1.

As we’ve already shown in C.1:

‖∂𝐀∂𝐓‖2≤1L.\Big\|\frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{T}}\Big\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{L}.
‖𝐙1‖2=‖(𝐈L⊗𝐗⊤)​(∂𝐀/∂𝐓)​(𝐗⊗𝐗)‖2≤‖𝐗‖2​1L​‖𝐗‖22=1L​‖𝐗‖23\|\mathbf{Z}_{1}\|_{2}=\|(\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{X}^{\top})\,(\partial\mathbf{A}/\partial\mathbf{T})\,(\mathbf{X}\otimes\mathbf{X})\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}\,\frac{1}{L}\,\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{L}\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{3}
‖∂2𝐀∂𝐓2‖2≤6,‖𝐙2‖2≤‖𝐗‖25​‖∂2𝐀∂𝐓2‖2≤6​‖𝐗‖25,\Big\|\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{T}^{2}}\Big\|_{2}\leq 6,\qquad\|\mathbf{Z}_{2}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{5}\Big\|\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{A}}{\partial\mathbf{T}^{2}}\Big\|_{2}\leq 6\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{5},
‖𝐀‖2≤L​L​‖𝐀‖max=L.\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{LL}\,\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\max}=L.

Therefore ‖𝐀𝐗‖2≤‖𝐀‖2​‖𝐗‖2≤L​‖𝐗‖2\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}\leq L\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2} (Property 10).

We also use the attention curvature blocks 𝚽k​ℓ\bm{\Phi}_{k\ell} from Lemma 2. Using Properties 10, 9 and the bounds on ‖𝐙1‖2\|\mathbf{Z}_{1}\|_{2}, ‖𝐙2‖2\|\mathbf{Z}_{2}\|_{2} above, we have (again similarly to C.1)

‖𝚽V​V‖2=0,\displaystyle\|\bm{\Phi}_{VV}\|_{2}=0,
‖𝚽Q​Q‖2≤2L​dV​dK​‖𝐖V‖2​‖𝐖K‖2​‖𝐙2‖2​‖𝐖K‖2≤12L​dV​dK​‖𝐖V‖2​‖𝐖K‖22​‖𝐗‖25,\displaystyle\|\bm{\Phi}_{QQ}\|_{2}\leq\frac{2}{Ld_{V}d_{K}}\,\|\mathbf{W}_{V}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{W}_{K}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{Z}_{2}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{W}_{K}\|_{2}\leq\frac{12}{Ld_{V}d_{K}}\|\mathbf{W}_{V}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{W}_{K}\|_{2}^{2}\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{5},
‖𝚽V​Q‖2≤2L​dV​dK​‖𝐈L⊗𝐒‖2​‖𝐙1‖2​‖𝐈dV⊗𝐖K‖2≤2L2​dV​dK​‖𝐖K‖2​‖𝐗‖23,\displaystyle\|\bm{\Phi}_{VQ}\|_{2}\leq\frac{2}{Ld_{V}\sqrt{d_{K}}}\,\|\mathbf{I}_{L}\otimes\mathbf{S}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{Z}_{1}\|_{2}\,\|\mathbf{I}_{d_{V}}\otimes\mathbf{W}_{K}\|_{2}\leq\frac{2}{L^{2}\sqrt{d_{V}d_{K}}}\|\mathbf{W}_{K}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{3},
